name: House of Bourbon-Parma
summary:
The House of Bourbon-Parma, a cadet branch of the Spanish Bourbon dynasty created when Philip V of Spain obtained the Duchy of Parma for his son Charles (1731) — later exchanged for the Kingdom of Naples — and then assigned Parma to his younger son Philip (1748), is the most recently active of the historic Bourbon dynasties, with members currently serving as Grand Duke and Grand Duchess of Luxembourg (since 1964). Despite governing a small north Italian duchy (1748-1859, 1854-1859), the Bourbon-Parma produced European royalty who married into nearly every major dynasty.

The Duchy of Parma under the Bourbon-Parma was known for Enlightenment-influenced reforms: Ferdinand I (r. 1765-1802) invited French encyclopedists and implemented physiocratic economic reforms; his wife Marie-Amélie of Austria (daughter of Maria Theresa) brought Austrian administrative efficiency. Napoleon incorporated Parma into France (1802), but it was restored as a Bourbon duchy in 1814, then gained by Marie Louise of Austria (Napoleon's wife) until 1847, then returned to the Bourbons. The 1859 Risorgimento (Italian unification) ended Bourbon-Parma rule in Italy.

The dynasty's most consequential modern member: Robert I (r. 1854-1859), the last Duke of Parma, had 24 children who married into almost every European royal family. His granddaughter Zita of Bourbon-Parma (1892-1989) married Emperor Karl I of Austria (the last Habsburg), making the Bourbon-Parma the in-laws of the last Habsburg emperor; Zita's son Otto von Habsburg (1912-2011) was the Habsburg pretender and a founder of the European Union's conceptual framework. Grand Duke Henri of Luxembourg (b. 1955) is the current dynasty's reigning representative.
